questions.enonce_markdown:
Assess the full implication of the call of Samuel.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The call of Samuel is told in 1 Samuel 3. Samuel, born to Hannah in answer to prayer and dedicated to the service of God at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1), was a boy serving under the priest Eli when God called him. To 'assess' its full implication is to judge its importance for Samuel himself, for Eli, and for Israel.

**1. The setting.** The narrator says that the word of the LORD was rare in those days and that visions were not widespread. The priesthood at Shiloh was corrupt, since Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas abused their position. The call is therefore God's answer to a religious and moral crisis.

**2. The call.** During the night God called Samuel by name. Three times he went to Eli, thinking that Eli had called. Eli then understood that it was God and told him to answer, 'Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening'. This shows that revelation depended on the attitude of obedience and listening.

**3. Implications for Samuel.**
(i) *He became a prophet.* The narrator says that all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was a trustworthy prophet of the LORD, and that the LORD continued to reveal Himself to him at Shiloh.
(ii) *A hard first task.* The first message was a judgement on the house of Eli, which Samuel had to deliver to the man who had brought him up. It tested his honesty and courage.
(iii) *A lifelong ministry.* He served as prophet, judge and priestly figure, leading Israel at Mizpah (1 Samuel 7), and was later the one who anointed Saul and then David.

**4. Implications for Eli and the priesthood.** The message announced the end of Eli's family line in the priesthood because the sons were not restrained. Eli accepted it humbly. The judgement was fulfilled in 1 Samuel 4 when Israel was defeated by the Philistines, the ark was captured and Hophni and Phinehas died.

**5. Implications for Israel.** (i) The renewal of the prophetic word after a period of silence. (ii) A change of leadership, from a corrupt priesthood to the prophet as the main channel of God's word. (iii) The beginning of the transition from the age of the Judges to the monarchy, since Samuel would guide Israel in that change.

**6. Religious lessons.** God calls even the young and the humble; He holds leaders accountable; revelation requires listening and obedience; truth must be spoken even when it is costly.

**Conclusion.** The call of Samuel was far more than a personal experience: it renewed the prophetic voice, ended the line of Eli and prepared the way for the monarchy.
